## What peer review does

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
### Transactional

- Vets knowledge
- Gatekeeps
- Routes work to venues
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
### Discursive

- Gives authors feedback
- Sustains argument
- Builds community and mentors
:::
:::

## Where it happens

- Journal review
- Internal institutional review
- Informal review among friends
- Open platforms such as F1000 and PeerJ
- Blogs and social media
- Journal clubs, including this one

## Why AI is entering peer review

- Submissions grow faster than the pool of reviewers
- Editors struggle to find reviewers, and reviewing earns little credit
- More than half of researchers already use AI in peer review, often against guidance (Naddaf 2025, *Nature*)

## The review pipeline

::: {.src}
Wu et al. 2026, ACL
:::

::: {.flow}
<span class="step">Review</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Rebuttal</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Meta-review</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Decision</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Revision</span>
:::

The survey covers generating reviews, rebuttals, and meta-reviews, and revising papers from reviews. Review generation has received the most attention.

## How systems are built

::: {.src}
Wu et al. 2026, ACL
:::

- Fine-tuning on corpora of expert reviews
- Multi-agent systems that split a review into roles such as novelty checking and weakness diagnosis
- Reinforcement learning against rewards for criticism, relevance, and actionability
- Retrieval and iterative refinement to ground comments

## Evaluation methods

::: {.src}
Wu et al. 2026, ACL
:::

| Approach | Yardstick | Weakness |
|----------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Human-centric | Expert and user ratings, pairwise preference | Costly and subjective |
| Reference-based | Overlap with human-written reviews | Shallow; treats human reviews as ground truth |
| LLM-based | LLM judges | Position, verbosity, and style bias |
| Aspect-oriented | Novelty, clarity, error types | Heavy annotation; no single score |

## Reported limitations

::: {.src}
Wu et al. 2026, ACL
:::

- LLMs mimic reviewer tone but remain weak at judging novelty
- Zero-shot output tends to be generic and overly positive
- Systems are open to manipulation through injection attacks
- Models can favour authors from highly ranked institutions
- Most datasets come from NLP and ML venues

::: {.notes}
The survey cites a study estimating that 6.5 to 16.9 percent of review text at top AI venues was substantially modified by LLMs. It closes by calling for explicit disclosure of any LLM use in review.
:::

## Trust and effort

::: {.src}
Pilatti et al. 2026, Ethics & Behavior
:::

- Peer review is a social technology, a pact of trust linking competence, confidentiality, and accountability
- Generative AI makes plausible evaluative text cheap to produce, while the reviewer's actual thinking stays hard to observe
- Workload, speed, and competition drive adoption, so the authors treat AI-assisted review as difficult to reverse

::: {.notes}
Scoping review, qualitative analysis of recent literature and institutional policies.
:::

## Accountability laundering

::: {.src}
Pilatti et al. 2026, Ethics & Behavior
:::

- Effort outsourcing and accountability laundering is the first of the three risks the review identifies
- Generative AI makes plausible, well-structured evaluative text cheap, while the reasoning behind it stays weakly observable
- Reviewer effort and AI use are both hard to detect, so a reviewer can sign a report without anyone knowing how much of the judgement was theirs

::: {.notes}
Buriak et al. state the counterpart: a computer has no integrity or moral compass and cannot be held accountable.
:::

## The other two risks

::: {.src}
Pilatti et al. 2026, Ethics & Behavior
:::

- AI-generated review reports are difficult to detect
- Adversarial attacks such as prompt injection hidden in manuscripts

## Auditable hybrid governance

::: {.src}
Pilatti et al. 2026, Ethics & Behavior
:::

The goal is to make AI-assisted workflows verifiable without relying only on bans or text policing.

- Reviewer accountability
- Granular disclosure of the tasks and content AI processed
- Evidence-anchored auditing, with critiques tied to specific sections of the manuscript
- Confidentiality
- Secure infrastructure

::: {.notes}
The first three components target laundering by making the reviewer's own work checkable. The detail on disclosure and anchored critiques comes from the Open Scholarship Policy Observatory's summary of the paper.
:::

## Why reviewers are chosen

::: {.src}
Buriak et al. 2026, ACS Nano
:::

- Editors choose a particular reviewer for that person's expertise, perspective, and evaluation
- Reports clearly written by generative AI are still infrequent but growing, and they are superficial and error prone
- Each one slows the process, because the editors have to seek out a new reviewer

::: {.notes}
The editors say they could have generated a review with ChatGPT themselves if they had wanted one. The editorial cites a December 2025 survey suggesting more than half of reviewers use AI assistance. Its position is that peer review is a human responsibility that cannot be delegated to AI.
:::

## What LLMs can and cannot do

::: {.src}
Buriak et al. 2026, Figure 1
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
### LLMs and humans

- Research summary
- Grammar and spelling
- Syntax
- Inconsistencies
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
### Humans only

- Novelty assessment
- Critical thinking
- Experimental logic
- Data and graphics analysis
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The figure marks humans as capable of all eight tasks. The text adds that LLMs trained on existing literature may steamroll imaginative work, that they cannot yet analyze figures or evaluate the primary data in Supporting Information, and that they hallucinate citations and data. The editors doubt any existing LLM will identify breakthroughs or creative insight.
:::

## Confidentiality and accountability

::: {.src}
Buriak et al. 2026, ACS Nano
:::

- Uploading a manuscript to an LLM breaches confidentiality and is prohibited at ACS journals, no different from sharing a manuscript under review with a colleague or friend
- The editors also do not support checking a draft report with an LLM, since a detailed review can indirectly disclose the science in the manuscript
- A computer has no integrity or moral compass and cannot be held accountable

::: {.notes}
The editors also raise intellectual property. Many LLMs are built by commercial entities with research interests in the same fields, and nobody can know what happens to uploaded material.
:::

## What a good review does

::: {.src}
Buriak et al. 2026, ACS Nano
:::

- Gives a balanced report that emphasizes the scientific value of the work and explains the basis for the assessment
- Tells hype apart from creative advance, which the editors call a judgement skill that stays in the human realm
- Remembers that authors are people, often students meeting peer review for the first time, and rereads for tone
- Keeps requests for new experiments reasonable, since the reviewer is not the research director of the work

::: {.notes}
The section on a responsible role for AI points to the authors' 2023 editorial on using AI when writing manuscripts: properly prompted AI can spark creativity, give quick access to information, and help non-native English speakers with grammar in a draft. It rules out using an LLM to check a draft review. The conclusion accepts that LLMs are widely accessible and asks the community to work out how to use them while protecting peer review. The dangers section lists harms to authors, reviewers, editors, students and early career researchers, and the scientific community, including homogenization of science.
:::

## What each paper asks

| Paper | Asks |
|------------|------------------------------|
| Wu et al. | What AI can do, and how anyone would know |
| Pilatti et al. | Who stays accountable when review effort is outsourced |
| Buriak et al. | What must stay human |
